title: How to Read a Book: The Classic Guide to Intelligent Reading
author: Mortimer J. Adler and Charles Van Doren
target_audience: Students seeking to improve reading comprehension and critical thinking
Anyone seeking to get more from reading nonfiction and fiction
core_themes: Active reading as an intellectual discipline
The art of questioning and understanding texts
The importance of lifelong, self-directed learning
Reading as a means of intellectual growth
primary_purpose: To teach readers how to systematically approach any book, engage deeply with its arguments, ideas, and structure, and ultimately become an active, critically-thinking reader capable of extracting maximum understanding and value from any text.

structure_format.narrative_style: Instructional, structured, and methodical with a clear, scholarly tone
structure_format.organization: Divided into four parts: The Dimensions of Reading; The Third Level of Reading: Analytical Reading; Approaches to Different Kinds of Reading Matter; The Ultimate Goals of Reading
features: Practical exercises and questions to apply strategies
Summaries and diagrams illustrating reading methods
Comparative analyses of reading different genres

key_concepts_lessons: Reading is an active process involving questioning, clarifying, and synthesizing ideas.
There are four levels of reading: Elementary, Inspectional, Analytical, and Syntopical.
Analytical reading requires identifying an author’s main arguments, terms, propositions, and evaluating their validity.
Reading approaches differ based on the genre and purpose—practical books, imaginative literature, plays, poetry, history, science, and philosophy all require special techniques.
Syntopical (comparative) reading lets you confront and synthesize multiple texts on a subject.
Asking the right questions is key to critical and intelligent reading.
notable_features: Introduction of the four levels of reading model
Guidance for reading a wide range of texts, from novels and philosophy to science and social sciences
Comprehensive checklists for analytical and syntopical reading
cultural_historical_context: Originally published in 1940 and updated in 1972, the book addresses the problem of superficial reading and the decline of critical thinking, advocating for intellectual rigor during a time of educational change and rapidly increasing access to information.
reception_impact: Regarded as a classic and foundational work on critical reading and learning
Frequently cited in academic circles and recommended in university curricula
Valued by autodidacts and lifelong learners
Praised for its clarity and comprehensive approach to reading
Some readers find the tone dense or academic
comparable_titles: The Well-Educated Mind: A Guide to the Classical Education You Never Had by Susan Wise Bauer
A Rulebook for Arguments by Anthony Weston
How to Think: A Survival Guide for a World at Odds by Alan Jacobs
